I share a hostel room with Nandini, so I saw the whole scholarship essay thing up close.
On Monday night she sat on her bed with the laptop and typed without stopping for about forty minutes. No backspacing that I could hear. When I asked if she wanted tea, she said, "Not now, Sarika, I'm writing badly on purpose." Then she shut the laptop and went to sleep.
Tuesday she didn't open it at all. Went to class, played badminton, normal.
On Wednesday morning she printed it and sat on the floor with a red pen. She crossed out whole lines. At one point she laughed out loud at something she had written. By lunch the essay was a page shorter.
I've seen other people in our wing stare at a blank screen for days, or rewrite one paragraph thirty times. Nandini looked almost relaxed. I don't know what was going on inside, but she submitted it that Friday.

qa.q: What did Nandini do on Wednesday morning?
qa.a: She printed it and sat on the floor with a red pen.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel watching Nandini's way of working?
qa.a: Sarika seemed curious and a bit impressed, comparing Nandini's calm with others who stare at a blank screen or rewrite endlessly.

qa.q: Which part of Nandini's process could help a writer who freezes at a blank page?
qa.a: Writing a fast rough draft on purpose without fixing anything, because it separates making the draft from judging it.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when she laughed at her own draft?
qa.a: Nandini probably felt amused and relaxed, seeing the rough draft with fresh eyes instead of fearing it.

grounding: An observer describes a student who writes a rough draft without judging, leaves it for a day and then edits with fresh eyes.

Friday. The college magazine wanted Lokesh's article on the new bus route by Tuesday. He opened a blank page at nine and stared at it. At eleven he had one sentence, and he had deleted it six times. He went to bed feeling sick.
Saturday. Vandana, the senior editor, found him in the library. "You're editing before anything exists," she said. "Write the worst version. Twenty minutes. No deleting." He set a timer. It was clumsy and repetitive, but at the end there were three pages. She told him not to look at it again till Monday.
Monday. Lokesh opened the file with coffee and read it like a stranger's. He could suddenly see the two good paragraphs and the four lazy ones. He cut a page, moved the best line to the top and sent it to Vandana by noon. She sent back one comment: "Now it sounds like you."

qa.q: How many times had Lokesh deleted his one sentence by eleven?
qa.a: He had deleted it six times.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on Friday night?
qa.a: Lokesh felt frightened and stuck, going to bed feeling sick after two hours with a blank page.

qa.q: Which step made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Writing the worst version for twenty minutes with no deleting, and then waiting till Monday, because making and judging were finally kept apart.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Lokesh's final article?
qa.a: Vandana seems pleased; her comment "Now it sounds like you" shows she thinks the rest and the edit brought out his own voice.

grounding: Shows a young writer who breaks blank-page fear by drafting roughly without judging, resting, then editing with fresh eyes.

passage:
Yusuf, you want to be a writer? Then let your old uncle Lalit tell you what my first editor did to me.
I was a trainee reporter at the district paper, barely out of college. My first story was about a bridge that had cracked. I sat until midnight polishing the first line. Twenty versions. The rest of the page was empty. I was terrified it wasn't good enough.
Mr Bhatia, the editor, came past, took my pen and said, "Write it ugly. All of it. Then go home and sleep." I was offended, beta! But I did it. Ugly, fast, all of it.
At seven the next morning he handed it back. "Now read it as if someone else wrote it." I saw the mistakes at once. The good line was in the fourth paragraph, not the first. I fixed it in forty minutes.
I used that method for thirty-one years.

qa.q: What was Lalit's first story about?
qa.a: It was about a bridge that had cracked.

qa.q: What was young Lalit feeling at midnight with only a polished first line?
qa.a: Lalit was terrified the story wasn't good enough, stuck polishing one line twenty times.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Writing it ugly, sleeping, and then reading it as someone else's work, because the rest let Lalit see where the good line really was.

qa.q: How might Mr Bhatia have seen the young reporter that night?
qa.a: Mr Bhatia probably saw a nervous beginner stuck in endless polishing, and cared enough to push him to finish and rest.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to write a rough draft fast, sleep on it and then edit with fresh eyes.

Eshaan was on the 7:40 local, squeezed against the door, when Kavitha's message arrived. The network kept dropping, so it loaded in pieces.
"Hi! So about Thursday, the client said maybe the meeting moves, or maybe not, they were unsure about the room, also Pradeep might join, and the deck needs a few changes, not sure which, and they mentioned the budget sheet? Anyway let me know!!"

He guessed. At the office he spent an hour updating the budget sheet and emailed it to the client.
At noon Kavitha called. "Why did you send them the budget? I only needed you to check if you were free on Thursday."
Eshaan put the phone down and rubbed his eyes. An hour gone, and an awkward email to take back.

In the accounts office in Koramangala, Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails. Himani's was the longest.
It began with how the audit had gone last year, moved on to a vendor who was always late, mentioned a spreadsheet "somewhere on the shared drive," and ended with three questions tangled in one paragraph. Anjali scrolled down, scrolled up, and still could not tell whether Himani wanted numbers, a meeting or just to vent.
She flagged it. Later, she told herself. Later became two days.
On Thursday Himani messaged, "Did you see my email? It's urgent." Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt. She opened the email again, took a pen and wrote on a sticky note: "Question 1? Question 2? Deadline?" It took her twenty minutes to pull the three questions apart.
She replied with three numbered answers and one line at the end: "Next time, could you put the questions at the top?"

qa.q: How many unread emails did Anjali have?
qa.a: Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel when Himani messaged that it was urgent?
qa.a: Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt, because she had delayed the unclear email for two days.

qa.q: What small request at the end could help both of them next time?
qa.a: Asking Himani to put the questions at the top, so the reader does not have to dig them out.

qa.q: How might the delay have looked from Himani's side?
qa.a: Himani was probably worried and impatient, not knowing that her long email was the reason no reply came.

"Sure. What's up?"

1. Pay Sharma Traders on 15 March, ₹48,000, invoice in the 'March' folder.
2. Do NOT pay Nair Supplies until they send the corrected invoice.

Anand, the new secretary of Laxmi Nagar Housing Society in Pune, had written his first notice about the water tank cleaning. It filled a whole page. It explained the history of the tank, a complaint from last year, the name of the cleaning company, and near the bottom, the actual dates.
He read it aloud to his neighbour Gautam over tea on the landing.
Gautam listened, then asked, "So when is there no water?"
Anand found the line. It was in the second-last paragraph. He laughed at himself.
They sat with a pencil. Anand read each sentence aloud; if Gautam didn't need it, it went. The page became six lines:
"No water: Saturday 14 June, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. (tank cleaning).
Please store water on Friday night.
Lift will run as usual.
Questions: Anand, Flat B-204."
He printed it and stuck it by the lift. On Saturday, not one resident knocked on his door to ask.

qa.q: Where did Anand stick the notice?
qa.a: He printed it and stuck it by the lift.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Gautam asked when there was no water?
qa.a: Anand felt a bit embarrassed but amused, laughing at himself when he found the key line near the bottom.

qa.q: Which method turned the page into six lines, and why does it work?
qa.a: Reading each sentence aloud and cutting what the reader didn't need, because it shows the notice from the reader's side.

qa.q: How might the residents see the final notice?
qa.a: They would find it easy to act on, which is why nobody needed to knock and ask on Saturday.

grounding: Shows a writer who reads a notice aloud, cuts it hard and puts the date, time and action first.

"Samir, can you look at this before I send it to the director?" Shalini turned her screen.
Samir read for a moment. "What do you want her to do?"
"Approve two more interns for the summer."
"Where does it say that?"
Shalini scrolled. "Paragraph four."
"Put it first. Line one: 'Request: approval for two summer interns, June to August.'"
"Won't that sound rude?"
"It sounds clear. Then why, in two short sentences. Numbers, not adjectives."
"So not 'a heavy workload'?"
"'Three new clients, forty extra hours a week.' Then the exact action at the end."
"'Please approve by Friday so we can post the listing on Monday.'"
"Good. Now read the whole thing aloud."
Shalini read. Halfway through she stopped. "This paragraph about last year is… not needed."
"Cut it."
She cut it, and two more lines. "It's a third shorter."
"And twice as likely to get a yes," Samir said.

qa.q: How many summer interns is Shalini asking for?
qa.a: Approval for two summer interns, June to August.

qa.q: Why did Shalini worry about putting the request first?
qa.a: Shalini was worried it would sound rude to the director to start with the ask.

qa.q: What steps did Samir suggest to make the email better?
qa.a: Put the request first, give reasons with numbers in short sentences, end with the exact action and date, then read it aloud and cut.

qa.q: How might the director feel reading the shorter email?
qa.a: The director would likely feel it is easy to decide on, since the request, reason and deadline are clear in seconds.

grounding: Illustrates a writer who learns to state the point first, use short sentences with numbers, end with the exact action and cut a third by reading aloud.

It had rained all night, so the assembly moved into the small hall, and the microphone died.
Harsha stood at the front with his poem. His heart was banging. His mouth felt like cotton. He said the first line. Then nothing. The second line had gone.
A boy giggled. Harsha's face burned. Gautam sir quietly walked up and said the first word of the line. Harsha finished, too fast and too soft, and ran back to his place.
That week Gautam sir asked him to say the poem only to him, in the empty classroom. Then to three friends at lunch. Then to his little sister at home. On Monday he said it to the class from his own desk. His hands still shook a little. He didn't forget a single line.

qa.a: It had rained all night.

The Class Ten room at the government school in Rajgarh had one borrowed projector, a sheet pinned to the wall and a fan that kept stopping. Leela's group was presenting on solar water pumps.
Leela had made the slides herself, and she had put everything on them: twelve lines per slide, small letters. When it was her turn, she turned to face the sheet and read. Her voice was steady, but her back was to the class.
By the third slide, the boys at the back were drawing on each other's hands. Two girls whispered. Irfan sir tapped his pen.
Then the power cut off. The sheet went blank. Leela stood there, heart thumping. Irfan sir said, "Just tell us. How does the pump work?"
She turned around. She talked about her uncle's farm and the pump he got last year, how the water came on at noon. The back row stopped drawing. When the power came back, she didn't turn to the screen again.

qa.q: How many lines did Leela put on each slide?

In Vancouver, Chen's Grade Nine science presentation on honeybees had eighteen slides. Each one was packed with sentences he had copied from his notes.
He stood beside the screen, clicker in hand, and read. He did not look up once. Reading felt safe; if the words were there, he couldn't go blank.
From his seat, Kofi watched the room. By slide seven, two people had their heads on their desks. Kofi himself had read ahead and was already on slide nine in his head.
Afterwards, Ms Laurent's feedback note said: "Excellent research. But I could read it myself. What do YOU think is the most surprising thing about bees?" Chen stared at the question. He knew the answer: that they dance to show each other where flowers are. It wasn't on any slide.
For the next project, he put one picture per slide and a few words. He practised telling it to his mom at dinner.

qa.q: How many slides did Chen's presentation have?
qa.a: It had eighteen slides.

qa.q: Why did Chen read every slide without looking up?
qa.a: Chen felt nervous about going blank, and reading felt safe because the words were there.

Supervisor's note, final-year seminar series, week 6.
Sudha presented her project on rainwater harvesting today. It was well organised. About four minutes in, she said "catchment" wrongly, paused, corrected it and went on. The rest was confident.
Afterwards she came to my desk looking close to tears. "Everyone heard that. They'll remember it as the girl who can't say 'catchment.'"
I asked her to wait. When the class returned from the break, I asked them, without naming anyone, to write down one thing they remembered from each talk. On Sudha's, eleven of fourteen wrote about the rooftop tank photo. Nobody mentioned the word. Rekha, who presented after her, wrote only "I was too nervous about mine to notice much."
I showed Sudha the slips. She read them twice and let out a long breath.
I will repeat this exercise with the next group; it helps.
— Seminar supervisor

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she came to the desk?
qa.a: Sudha was upset and ashamed, close to tears and sure everyone had noticed and would remember the mistake.

qa.q: Which choice by the supervisor worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to write what they remembered, because it showed Sudha real evidence that the stumble went unnoticed.

qa.q: What was the seminar like for Rekha?

grounding: Shows a student sure that a small stumble was noticed and remembered, and evidence that the audience noticed far less.

Thursday night.
Viva today. First question, easy. Second question, I said "resistance" when I meant "resistor." The external examiner raised one eyebrow, I corrected myself, and we moved on.
I have replayed that eyebrow maybe fifty times since. I'm sure the examiner wrote it down. I'm sure Samir, who was waiting by the door, heard. By dinner I had decided that everyone in the lab now thinks I don't know basic circuits.
Then I actually asked Samir. He looked blank. "What mistake?" He'd been standing there going over his own answers in his head, terrified about the transistor question.
Also: my marks are up on the portal. Good grade.
So the whole lab was not thinking about me. The examiner had probably seen that slip a hundred times. Everyone was busy with their own nerves.
Note to self, Kashish: next viva, correct it and move on. Nobody's keeping a list.

qa.a: The narrator said "resistance."

qa.q: How did Kashish feel in the hours after the viva?
qa.a: Kashish felt anxious and embarrassed, replaying the examiner's eyebrow about fifty times.

qa.q: What did Kashish learn to do next time?
qa.a: Correct the slip and move on, remembering that listeners notice far less than it feels.

In a small lecture room in Seoul, Soo-ah stood up to present her exchange-year project to the language club. She had practised for a week. As soon as she began, her voice shook. She could hear it herself: thin, wobbly.
She looked at the back wall and felt her throat tighten. Then, in the front row, she noticed Esther. Esther was leaning forward, nodding slowly at each sentence, as if she really wanted to hear what came next.
Soo-ah looked at her. Nodded back, almost without meaning to. Took a breath. The next sentence came out steadier. By the third slide she was looking around the room, and her voice had settled.
Afterwards, Esther came up. "Your part about the market was great. I was nervous for you at the start, you know. I just wanted you to know someone was listening."
Soo-ah hugged her, surprising them both.

In the college seminar room, Irfan's slides were ready, but his voice was not. "Good… good morning," he began, and it cracked. A few people shifted. He felt heat climb up his neck. The next sentence came out in a rush.
In the second row sat Tushar, who had shared a lab bench with him all year. Tushar caught his eye, gave a small nod and tapped his own chest twice, slowly: breathe.
Irfan stopped. Took a breath. Looked down at his first slide, then back at Tushar, who nodded again.
"Sorry. Let me start again," Irfan said. "Our project is about why some bridges crack in winter."
This time his voice held. Other people started nodding too. By the end, someone asked a question, and he answered it without looking at his notes.
Later, over tea, Irfan said, "That chest tap saved me." Tushar shrugged. "Everyone's been there."

qa.q: What is Irfan's project about?
qa.a: Our project is about why some bridges crack in winter.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when his voice cracked?
qa.a: Irfan felt embarrassed and panicky, with heat climbing up his neck as the next sentence came out in a rush.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: Tushar nodded and tapped his chest twice to say breathe, a small kind signal that let Irfan pause and restart calmly.

qa.q: How does Tushar see Irfan's nerves?
qa.a: Tushar feels sympathy rather than judgment, shrugging that everyone's been there.

grounding: Shows a nervous speaker whose cracking voice is met by a friend's attentive nod and calming gesture, helping him recover.

Dear Devika,
I don't think you know what you did on Saturday, so I'm writing it down.
When I stood up to speak at the hostel farewell, my voice shook so badly I thought I would have to sit down. I could hear it wobbling. My note card was trembling in my hand. I was sure everyone was cringing.
Then I saw you in the third row. You weren't looking at your phone. You were looking at me, and every time I finished a sentence, you nodded a little, like you were saying "yes, go on." I started talking to you instead of to the whole room. By the time I got to the part about our warden's tea, my voice was mine again, and people were laughing in the right places.
Afterwards three juniors said it was the best speech of the evening. Half of that is yours.
Thank you, really.
Farida

qa.q: Where was Devika sitting?
qa.a: In the third row.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when the speech began?
qa.a: Farida felt frightened and exposed, with a shaking voice and trembling note card, sure everyone was cringing.

qa.q: What did Farida do after spotting Devika's nodding?
qa.a: Farida started talking to Devika instead of the whole room, which steadied the voice until it felt normal again.

qa.q: How might Devika feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Devika would probably feel surprised and touched, since Devika may not have known the nodding made such a difference.

grounding: Illustrates a nervous speaker whose shaking voice steadies because one audience member keeps nodding kindly.

Week one. Chinmay sat in the Monday review as Tushar went through forty slides of sales data. Tables, then more tables. By slide twelve Chinmay realised he had stopped reading and was thinking about lunch. He felt a bit guilty and tried to focus again. He couldn't find the thread.
Week two. Same meeting, thirty-five slides. Chinmay noticed the manager scrolling on her phone. When Tushar asked, "Any questions?", nobody had one. Chinmay wanted to ask what the main point was, but it felt rude.
Week three. On Wednesday, the manager stopped Chinmay in the corridor. "What did Tushar's review say about the south region?" Chinmay tried. He remembered one chart, a red line going down in March, and Tushar saying, "That's the store that closed." That was all. Forty slides, and one sentence stayed.
That afternoon Chinmay messaged Tushar: "Can I show you something about your deck?"

qa.a: Tushar went through forty slides of sales data.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in week two when nobody had a question?
qa.a: Chinmay felt uneasy and hesitant, wanting to ask for the main point but worried it would seem rude.

qa.q: What could Chinmay show Tushar that might help his next deck?

qa.a: Tushar might feel surprised and a little hurt that all the detail was lost, but it could help him see what actually lands.

Vidya, you're giving your first big talk next week? Sit. Your Rajni aunty has a story.
When I was a young officer, maybe twenty-four, I was sent to a state conference on rural water. The main speaker was a senior engineer, very respected. He had brought sixty slides. Tables of pipe lengths, rainfall for every district, costs by year. He read them very fast.
I had a notebook. I tried to write. By the twentieth slide I had written only the date. The man next to me was asleep. I felt terrible for the engineer, and also, honestly, annoyed. I had taken a night bus to be there.
You know what I remember from that whole hour? One photograph. A girl carrying two pots on her head, and his one sentence: "She walks four kilometres. This project cuts it to two hundred metres."
Forty years later, I remember that girl. I don't remember a single table.

qa.q: What was the one photograph Rajni remembers?
qa.a: A girl carrying two pots on her head.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel as the slides went on?
qa.a: Rajni felt sorry for the engineer and also annoyed, having taken a night bus to be there.

qa.q: At what point in the talk did the engineer finally reach his audience?
qa.a: When he showed the photograph and said one clear sentence about the walk being cut to two hundred metres.

qa.q: How might the engineer have seen his own talk?
qa.a: The engineer probably thought all the tables showed how thorough the project was, not noticing that people had stopped following.

grounding: An elder recalls a talk full of detail with no clear message, where only one clear image and sentence were remembered.

The community hall in Hamilton was hot; the ceiling fans had broken the week before. Thomas had come straight from his shift to hear the council's plan for the flooded streets on his side of town.
Sonali, the council's planning officer, opened a laptop. Slide after slide: rainfall charts from 1998, pipe diameters, three alternative budgets, a map too small to read from the back. She spoke quickly, reading numbers aloud.
Thomas tried. He really did. His street flooded twice last winter. But after ten minutes he was fanning himself with the leaflet, and after twenty he was checking the time. Around him, people whispered to each other: "Are they fixing it or not?"
At the very end, Sonali said, "So, the Fourth Street drain gets replaced in spring." Thomas sat up. That was it. That was the thing he'd come for, in the last ten seconds.
Walking out, he heard three different people repeat that one line.

qa.q: Why was the community hall hot?
qa.a: The ceiling fans had broken the week before.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel as the slides went on?
qa.a: Thomas felt frustrated and restless, fanning himself and checking the time while trying to find the point.

qa.q: What could Sonali have done differently at the start?
qa.a: Sonali could have opened with the one clear message, that the Fourth Street drain gets replaced in spring, and kept the detail for questions.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the evening?
qa.a: Sonali may think she gave a thorough report, without realising most people only heard the last line.

grounding: Shows a listener who stops following a detail-heavy talk and remembers only the one clear point given at the end.

In Buenos Aires, Lucia had twelve minutes to convince a small foundation to fund her after-school reading club.
The night before, she wrote one sentence on a card: "Thirty kids read better in six months when someone reads with them twice a week." That was the message. Everything else had to support it.
She made four slides: a photo, one number, a simple chart, a budget. Then she practised aloud in the kitchen while her flatmate Kofi ate cereal and timed her. The first run took nineteen minutes. She cut. The third run took eleven.
At the meeting her hands were cold, but the card was in her pocket. When a board member asked how many kids stayed after the first month, Lucia said, "I don't know that number exactly. I'll check our register and email you by Friday."
The board member nodded and wrote something down. Lucia emailed on Thursday. The grant came through the next month.

qa.q: How many slides did Lucia make?
qa.a: She made four slides.

qa.q: How did Lucia feel at the meeting, and what steadied her?
qa.a: Lucia was nervous, with cold hands, but the card in her pocket with the main message steadied her.

qa.q: Which choice at the meeting built trust, and why?
qa.a: Saying honestly that she didn't know the exact number and promising to email by Friday, because it showed she wouldn't bluff.

qa.q: How did Kofi help Lucia's preparation?
qa.a: Kofi timed her practice runs in the kitchen, so Lucia could cut from nineteen minutes to eleven.

grounding: Illustrates a presenter who knows the main message, rehearses aloud, keeps slides light and admits honestly when she doesn't know.

At the bank's regional training centre, Vinita was to present the new loan-processing checklist to thirty branch staff. She had been a junior officer for a year and a half.
The week before, she had rehearsed aloud three times in the empty training room, timing herself on her phone. Her slides had one heading and three points each. Her main message was on the first slide: "The checklist cuts our processing from four days to two."
Halfway through, Madhav, the senior branch manager in the front row, raised his hand. "What happens to applications already in the system?"
Vinita felt her stomach drop. She didn't know. The room went quiet.
"That's a good question, sir. I don't know yet. I'll confirm with the head office and send the answer to everyone by Wednesday."
Madhav nodded. After the session, he came up. "Most people bluff on that one. I prefer your way."
She sent the answer on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Vinita's main message?
qa.a: The checklist cuts our processing from four days to two.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when Madhav asked the question?
qa.a: Vinita felt a sudden drop of fear, since she didn't know the answer and the room went quiet.

qa.q: What did Vinita do instead of bluffing, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Vinita said she didn't know yet and promised a confirmed answer by Wednesday, which kept her credible and calm.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Vinita's answer?
qa.a: Madhav respects it, saying most people bluff but he prefers her honest way.

grounding: Shows a presenter who rehearses aloud, keeps slides light, states the main message and answers a hard question honestly.

Dear Dhruv,
Masi told me you've got your first client presentation on Monday and you're not sleeping. I remember that feeling. So here's what worked for me, for what it's worth.
First, write your main message in one sentence. If you can't, you're not ready. Mine last month was, "We can move the launch up by two weeks if we drop the video."
Second, practise out loud. Not in your head. I did mine three times to my bathroom mirror, feeling ridiculous. The third time, I stopped needing notes.
Third, keep slides light. One idea each. People listen to you, not your slides.
Fourth, when they ask something you don't know, say so. Last month a client asked me about a supplier I'd never heard of. I said, "I don't know. I'll find out by tomorrow." They thanked me.
You'll be nervous anyway. That's fine. Prepared nervous is different.
Your cousin,
Lokesh

qa.q: How many times did Lokesh practise to the bathroom mirror?
qa.a: I did mine three times to my bathroom mirror.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel practising aloud to the mirror?
qa.a: Lokesh felt ridiculous at first, but by the third time felt steady enough not to need notes.

qa.q: Which of Lokesh's four tips might help Dhruv most on Monday, and why?
qa.a: Writing the main message in one sentence, because it tells Dhruv what everything else in the talk must support.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel reassured and less alone, knowing a cousin felt the same nerves and found a way through.

grounding: Illustrates a presenter who steadies nerves with a clear message, rehearsal aloud, light slides and honest answers to questions.

Come here, Chaitanya. You want to teach your little sister chess? Let your Sahil dada tell you something first.
When I was ten, I tried to teach my brother Anil marbles. He was six, and I was the champion of our lane. I shouted, "No! Flick with the thumb! Are you stupid?" He cried and ran to our mother.
I sat on the step, annoyed, trying to work out how to explain it. Then I realised I didn't know how I did it. My thumb just knew. So I shot slowly, watching my own hand. Knuckle down. Marble on the first finger. Thumb behind it.
Next day I showed Anil exactly that, three times, without shouting. He hit the ring on his fourth try. And I became a better player too.
Be patient with her, beta.

qa.q: What game did Sahil try to teach Anil?
qa.a: He tried to teach his brother Anil to play marbles.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel after Anil ran to their mother?
qa.a: Sahil felt annoyed and a little stuck, sitting on the step and trying to work out how to explain it better.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed the teaching?
qa.a: Sahil watched his own hand shooting slowly to find the real steps, then showed Anil calmly three times.

qa.q: How might Anil have felt when his brother shouted at him?
qa.a: Anil probably felt hurt and small, which is why he cried and ran to their mother.

grounding: An elder recalls teaching a younger sibling with impatience at first, and discovering how explaining clarified his own skill.

The power went out at eight, and the maths homework was due in the morning. Hafsa, eleven, sat at the kitchen table with a torch, helping her little brother Francis with fractions.
"No! Half is BIGGER than a quarter. How don't you know that?"
Francis pushed the book away. "You're shouting."
Hafsa glared at the ceiling. Then she took the last roti, tore it in two and held up a half. She tore the other piece again and held up a quarter. "Which would you rather eat?"
Francis pointed. "That one's bigger."
"Exactly." Hafsa stopped. She had only ever learned the rule; now she could see it. She drew the two roti pieces next to "½ > ¼".
When the lights came back, Francis did the next four himself. Hafsa did not say "finally," though she wanted to.

qa.q: What did Hafsa use to show Francis a half and a quarter?
qa.a: Hafsa tore the last roti into a half and a quarter.

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling when she shouted at Francis?
qa.a: Hafsa felt impatient and frustrated that Francis did not know something that seemed obvious.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than shouting, and why?
qa.a: Tearing the roti into a half and a quarter, because Francis could see the sizes, and it helped Hafsa understand the rule herself.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Hafsa shouted?
qa.a: Francis felt hurt and fed up, pushing the book away and saying "You're shouting."

grounding: Shows a child helping a younger brother with homework, mixing impatience with real help, and understanding the idea better herself by explaining.

In their flat in Lajpat Nagar, Ankita, nine, was teaching her little brother Lalit snakes and ladders.
"You roll, then you move. No, not that way! Ugh, give it." She moved his counter for him.
Lalit crossed his arms. "Then you play alone."
Ankita huffed and looked at the board. How did you explain which way to go? She traced it with her finger. Left, left, left, then up, then right, right, right. A zigzag. She had never noticed. She had only played.
"Lalit, look. It's a zigzag. Follow my finger." She let him move his own counter. When he climbed a ladder, she clapped louder than he did.
Their mother, in the kitchen, smiled at the clapping, though she also heard Ankita say "not like that" four more times.

qa.q: In which neighbourhood is the flat?
qa.a: In their flat in Lajpat Nagar.

qa.q: Why did Lalit cross his arms?
qa.a: Lalit felt annoyed and hurt that Ankita took over and moved his counter for him.

qa.q: How could Ankita keep helping without taking over?
qa.a: Ankita could keep letting Lalit move his own counter and show the zigzag with her finger instead of grabbing the board.

qa.q: How does their mother see the game from the kitchen?
